sections.html:
Around 33,254 people live in Warminster, spread over 14,014 households. Owners occupy about 69.3 percent of the homes. The midpoint value for an owned house is $418,600, and midpoint rent is $1,634 a month, so investors shop here as well as families.

Housing came late. In 1950 the township held 7,127 people, and by 1970 it held 34,900, which means the streets you will price against were mostly laid out in the postwar boom. About 27.1 percent of residents are 65 or older, so estate sales and downsizing sales show up often. Buyers of those older houses usually count on replacing kitchens, baths and mechanicals.

Warminster's Licenses and Inspections Department wants a permit when a property is altered, rented or sold. The application is filed online. Staff at 215-443-5423 can name the right permit if you phone before you apply.

A workable order of steps:

  • Phone or email the department ahead of listing to learn the permit name and the fee for a residential sale.
  • File the application in the online portal and pay there.
  • Ask if an inspection comes with the permit. If it does, book it and repair whatever it flags.
  • Hand a copy of the approved permit to your agent or settlement attorney so it lands in the closing file.

Begin early. Repairs eat calendar time, and your settlement date in the agreement of sale will not slide on its own. A buyer who wants the house as-is should tell you who will take care of the permit.

sections.h2: Transfer tax, recording and filing dates
sections.html:
Transfer tax is paid to the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds as the deed is filed. It is measured on the value conveyed, which can differ from the contract price, and your sales contract normally assigns the cost to buyer, seller or both. Personal checks are refused. Use cash at the office, a cashier's check, a money order or a card.

Warminster closing and assessment numbers
Closing or filing itemAmount or deadline
Total realty transfer tax2 percent of value
State portion1 percent
Municipality and school district portion1 percent
Homestead and farmstead filing deadlineMarch 1, for the tax year starting July 1
Buyer's contact details to the Board of Assessment AppealsWithin 30 days of purchase

Gifts inside a family may escape the tax. When the deed itself is silent about the exemption, the filer attaches the state's Statement of Value (REV-183), and your attorney or title agent usually prepares it.

sections.h2: Seller disclosure and the flood notice
sections.html:
Pennsylvania's seller disclosure law, 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303, requires you to give the buyer a signed statement about the property before the contract is signed. A newer layer is Act 74 of 2026: it creates a flood-insurance notice that sellers pass along after the Insurance Department publishes its flood information. Ask your agent or attorney when that reaches your contract.

The form wants only what you truly know about the roof, basement, plumbing and wiring. Be candid. A wrong answer can follow you past closing, so keep your own copy.

Assessment appeals are heard by the Bucks Board of Assessment Appeals. A change from an annual appeal begins with the tax year after the appeal. Call the Board to learn the filing cutoff for the year you plan to sell. If you live in the house, the homestead exclusion needs a filing by March 1. Your buyer, once the owner, must give the Board contact details within 30 days, which is worth a reminder when you sign.

sections.h2: Water contamination near the former Navy site
sections.html:
Some township wells were found to hold PFOS and PFOA that traced back to the former Navy site at Johnsville. The Navy paid for treatment systems, and the Warminster Municipal Authority now purchases extra water from the North Wales Water Authority. The Authority serves about 10,300 customers with water and sewer.

Buyers of a house on public water may bring it up. Keep a recent bill and the Authority's contact information in your folder, and send buyers to the Authority for its current water quality reports. A calm, factual answer keeps the question from derailing an offer.

Choose a listing when the house is in good shape and neighbors have sold lately. Choose an as-is cash sale when the house needs work or you are up against a deadline. Expect the cash number to come in under a repaired, listed price. Speed and fewer conditions are what you get back.

  • Get the offer in writing, with a closing date and evidence the buyer has the funds.
  • Learn whether the buyer will take the house before the township permit is issued, and who will pursue it.
  • Set the offer beside a net sheet for a listing, with permit costs and repairs counted in.

sections.h2: Getting an older Warminster house ready
sections.html:
Because most homes here date from the postwar build-out, inspectors tend to look hardest at the furnace, electrical panel, roof and plumbing. Walk through before you list. Note anything that was changed without a permit, since a buyer's inspector or lender may ask for the paperwork. If the budget is thin, tidy the obvious items and offer a credit for the larger ones instead of replacing a whole kitchen on a gamble.

Heirs face a particular choice. Emptying and updating a parent's house can take months, while a sale as-is hands that work to the buyer at a lower price. Weigh the carrying cost of taxes, utilities and insurance against what the repairs would return.

sections.h2: Documents to collect and what closing looks like
sections.html:
Start with your deed, newest tax bill, mortgage payoff statement and any records of permitted work. For an inherited house, add the papers proving who may sign. Keeping them together in one folder before you file the permit application saves repeated trips to the township and the title company.

A rough timeline: first week, call the township and collect papers. After that, book any inspection and decide between repairing and selling as-is. Once you have a contract, the title company orders payoff figures and drafts the deed, while the buyer side confirms the permit is in hand. At settlement you sign the deed and the title company files it with the county.

On that day the transfer tax is paid and your mortgage payoff is taken out of the proceeds. A cash sale has no lender appraisal and no financing condition, so the closing date is often yours to choose.

faqs.q: Does Warminster require a permit to sell a house?
faqs.a: Yes. Selling a property needs a permit from the Licenses and Inspections Department, filed online. Call 215-443-5423 first to confirm the permit type and fee.

faqs.q: What is a typical home value in Warminster?
faqs.a: The midpoint for an owned home is $418,600 for 2020 to 2024. Condition and nearby sales set your real price, so use the number only as a starting reference.

faqs.q: Should I mention the PFOS and PFOA wells to Warminster buyers?
faqs.a: Be ready to talk about it. The Warminster Municipal Authority closed wells hit by PFOS and PFOA from the former Navy site, installed treatment systems the Navy paid for, and buys more water from a neighboring authority. Send buyers to the Authority for current water quality reports.

faqs.q: Where do I record the deed for a Warminster house?
faqs.a: The Bucks County Recorder of Deeds, usually by way of your title company or attorney. The 2 percent transfer tax is collected at recording, and personal checks are refused.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Warminster house that I inherited?
faqs.a: Yes, after the person with authority over the estate signs. Pennsylvania's disclosure chapter exempts estate fiduciaries, although many sellers still hand over a condition statement. Ask the estate's attorney who may sign.
